what_would_change: Had the trace left the quoted route by more than 200 m for a stretch adding at least 0.2 km, RD-1 would apply and the extra kilometres would be weighed.

claims.assertion: This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total charged $28.97 with a distance component of 12.17 km at $1.4100/km), so detour kilometres feed directly into the fare and the RD-2 meter-service branch applies.

The GPS track records an off-route segment 09:04–09:14 where 5.23 km was driven against an optimal 1.08 km for that stretch, adding 4.15 km and reaching up to 1989 m away from the optimal route; under RD-1 that segment is an unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route.

No traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F14), and the only traffic records are speed band 3 (20–29 km/h) on EU TONG SEN STREET and SENTOSA GATEWAY (F12, F13); band 3 is not band 1 or 2, so RD-4 provides no justification for the 09:04–09:14 segment.

The complete, fully timestamped chat record contains only two messages — the rider's 08:47 pickup note and the driver's 08:48 ETA reply — with nothing from the rider about the route before the segment began at 09:04; there is therefore no rider consent of any kind for that segment.

The driver's post-trip statement that the GPS rerouted him (F11) is a bare claim with no traffic record behind it (F14) and cannot supply the consent that RD-5 requires from the rider's own message before the segment starts.

The excess mileage is what was billed: the fare fact prices 4.99 km of excess distance at $7.04 (4.99 km × $1.4100/km), and that is the distance component of the extra kilometres that RD-2 says is refundable for a metered trip.

The driver's 90-day record shows 3 disputes with 1 upheld, but neither upheld dispute was a route dispute (route: 0); because no prior route deviation has been upheld against him, the RD-6 repeat-offender flag is not available on this record.

The GPS trace's last sample is 4 minutes before drop-off, so the tail of the trip is unrecorded; the detour finding does not depend on that gap, because the off-route segment 09:04–09:14 sits wholly inside the covered stretch.

weaknesses: The off-route segment adds 4.15 km (F4) while the fare bills only 4.99 km of excess distance (F5) against the broader 10.2 km vs 7.2 km actual-vs-optimal difference (F2), so the driver can argue the refundable excess is the smaller of the two figures and that some of the gap is outside the segment.
The GPS trace stops 4 minutes before drop-off (F1), so part of the route is unrecorded; the driver can use this to argue the picture is incomplete, though it does not touch the 09:04–09:14 segment.

The driver's written assertion that the GPS app rerouted him (F11) is the kind of claim that can attract sympathy and suggests traffic-driven rerouting, even though RD-4 requires a traffic record (F14) and the only bands recorded are band 3 (F12, F13).
The driver is a long-standing, high-volume account (4.3 years, 677 trips in 90 days, F17), which the other side may use to argue this was a one-off navigation error rather than a pattern.
The rider's own profile shows 1 prior dispute in 90 days with 0 upheld (F16), which the driver side may cite to suggest the rider disputes fares readily.

The GPS record shows exactly one off-route segment, 09:04–09:14, where 5.23 km were driven against 1.08 km on the optimal route, adding 4.15 km (F4); total actual distance was 10.2 km vs 7.2 km optimal (F2), so the disputed excess is confined to that one segment.

points.response: Accepted: the trip is metered (F7), but that is precisely why the detour kilometres enter the fare — RD-2's RydeTAXI branch refunds the extra kilometres, and the meter legitimately bills only the distance properly driven.
Accepted, and it is fatal to the driver: the one off-route segment 09:04–09:14 (F4) is the unexplained deviation RD-1 prohibits, and 4.15 km of it is entirely inside the GPS-covered stretch.

Agreed on the record the driver himself states: the complete timestamped chat (F8, F9, F10) has no rider message about the route before 09:04, so the segment has no consent and the driver's post-trip reroute claim (F11) is a claim, not consent.

Conceded as against the driver: with no incident on the optimal route (F14) and only band-3 speeds on Eu Tong Sen Street and Sentosa Gateway (F12, F13), plus fair weather (F15), RD-4 exempts nothing and the segment falls to be refunded under RD-2.

The driver's own figure is the remedy: $7.04 of billed excess distance (F5), priced at the trip's $1.41/km rate that F7 confirms, is the RD-2 refund we ask for — the driver cannot bill extra kilometres and then keep the money for them.

The coverage gap (F1) does not help the driver: RD-2 refuses to refund the distance gap that is not attributed to a segment, and equally the segment at 09:04–09:14 (F4) needs no tail coverage to be a complete, self-contained deviation.
We join this concession: with zero route disputes upheld in 90 days (F17), RD-6's precondition of a prior upheld route dispute is unmet, so no account flag is requested.

Accepted: nothing in the chat, complaint or statement (F10, F11) is a threat or a dangerous-driving allegation, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation is not engaged and the rider's profile (F16) does not decide anything.

Conceded: the fare facts confirm this is a RydeTAXI metered trip whose distance component is billed at $1.4100/km (F7), so the RD-2 meter branch governs how much of the excess kilometrage can be refunded.
Conceded as to that segment: the record shows one off-route stretch 09:04–09:14 of 5.23 km against 1.08 km optimal, adding 4.15 km (F4); the segment is unexplained and my client does not dispute it.

Agreed — no incident is recorded near the route (F14) and the only bands are band 3, 20–29 km/h, on EU TONG SEN STREET and SENTOSA GATEWAY (F12, F13), which is not band 1 or 2, so RD-4 gives my client nothing for that segment.

Conceded: the chat record is complete and timestamped with only the rider's 08:47 pickup note and the driver's 08:48 reply (F8, F9, F10), so no rider message before 09:04 agrees to the segment and the ground is consent_after_or_none.
Conceded: my client's post-trip assertion that the GPS rerouted him (F11) is a claim, not the rider's own pre-segment message that RD-5 requires, and G11 bars treating it as consent.

The $7.04 figure is the billed excess distance (4.99 km × $1.4100/km, F5) and is not the measured segment excess: the off-route segment itself added 4.15 km (F4), and the remaining distance difference shown by the actual-vs-optimal comparison (F2) is not attributed to any `gps-detour-*` segment, so RD-2's ceiling is the segment's own extra kilometrage. A meter-component excess is refundable only up to the segment's extra_km × this trip's per-km rate — here 4.15 km × $1.41 ≈ $5.85 — which is below the $7.04 they ask; the judge should award the smaller, segment-matched amount.
Agreed: the driver has one upheld dispute in 90 days but zero route disputes upheld (F17), so there is no prior upheld route deviation and RD-6's repeated-violation flag is unavailable here.

Agreed that the 09:04–09:14 segment sits wholly inside the covered stretch (F4), so the untraced final 4 minutes (F1) neither adds nor removes any billed deviation kilometrage — it simply means no further segment can be found against my client.

I do not withdraw D6: the untraced tail (F1) and the fact that total actual distance exceeds optimal by 3.0 km while the single recorded segment adds 4.15 km (F2, F4) mean the record cannot tie every billed excess kilometre to a deviation, so refunding all 4.99 billed excess km (F5) would over-credit the rider beyond the segment the record proves.
